NG82 advises considering stopping anti VEGF treatment when the eye has severe, progressive visual loss despite treatment, and stopping when the eye develops late AMD (wet inactive) with no prospect of functional improvement [1]. Switching between anti VEGF agents may be considered for practical reasons, but clinical benefit from switching is likely to be limited [1]. People should be involved in every decision to stop or switch treatment [1]. Photodynamic therapy should not be offered alone for late AMD (wet active), and should not be offered as a first line adjunct to anti VEGF; as a second line adjunct it should be offered only within a randomised controlled trial [1]. Intravitreal corticosteroids should not be offered as an adjunct to anti VEGF, and thermal laser should not be offered for drusen in early AMD [1]. Treatment with anti VEGF should start as soon as possible, within 14 days of referral to the macular service, for eyes with confirmed late AMD (wet active) where antiangiogenic treatment is recommended [2]. Treatment with anti VEGF should start as soon as possible, within 14 days of referral to the macular service, for eyes with confirmed late AMD (wet active) where antiangiogenic treatment is recommended [1]. The VIEW 1 and VIEW 2 trials compared intravitreal aflibercept, including 2 mg every 8 weeks after three monthly loading doses, with monthly ranibizumab 0.5 mg in neovascular AMD [1]. At week 52 every aflibercept regimen was non inferior to monthly ranibizumab for maintaining vision, so aflibercept every 8 weeks achieved similar outcomes with fewer injections [1]. TENAYA and LUCERNE were two phase 3 randomised, double masked trials comparing faricimab given at intervals of up to every 16 weeks with aflibercept every 8 weeks in neovascular AMD [1]. Faricimab was non inferior to aflibercept for change in best corrected acuity at one year, and nearly half of faricimab treated eyes were on a 16 week interval at week 48 [1]. MARINA randomised people with minimally classic or occult choroidal neovascularisation due to AMD to monthly intravitreal ranibizumab 0.3 mg or 0.5 mg or sham injection for 24 months [1]. About 95 percent of ranibizumab treated eyes lost fewer than 15 letters at 12 months compared with about 62 percent of sham treated eyes, and mean acuity improved with ranibizumab while it declined with sham [1]. Treatment should continue only while an adequate response is maintained, and should stop with persistent deterioration in vision or anatomical changes showing an inadequate response [2]. The US label for tamsulosin warns that intraoperative floppy iris syndrome has been observed during cataract surgery in some patients treated with alpha one blockers [1]. The surgeon should be told before surgery, because the syndrome may need changes to surgical technique, and the benefit of stopping the drug before surgery has not been established [1]. NG77 advises that referral for cataract surgery should be based on the impact of the cataract on the person's vision and quality of life rather than on a visual acuity threshold, after discussion of the benefits and risks of surgery [2]. The US label for topiramate warns of a syndrome of acute myopia associated with secondary angle closure glaucoma, usually within the first month of treatment, presenting with acute reduced vision and ocular pain [1]. Treatment is to stop topiramate as rapidly as possible under the prescriber's judgement and to lower intraocular pressure [1].
